title: Homoscedasticity and Residual Diagnostics
summary: See the same data as a scatterplot and as residuals against fitted values. Dial the residual spread from flat to severe, and compare the classical and robust standard errors.
learningObjectives: Define homoscedasticity as approximately constant conditional residual variance.
Read a residuals-against-fitted-values plot, and explain why the horizontal axis must be fitted values rather than the outcome.
Explain why non-constant variance leaves the slope estimate unbiased while making its standard error untrustworthy.
Explain why the size and direction of that error depend on where the extra spread sits relative to the extremes of the predictor.
Treat a residual plot as a fallible diagnostic rather than a verdict, and say why a formal test does not settle it either.
interactionTypes: two linked views of one dataset
continuous manipulation of variance pattern and severity
residual spread compared across three regions
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every observation is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups, a number input and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the severity slider announces its meaning in words rather than as a bare percentage. The two-panel chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible four-row table giving the residual standard deviation in each third of the fitted values and the ratio of the widest to the narrowest, and a disclosure holds the intervals, tests, coverage and the exact model-implied standard error. Each panel is labelled in words inside the picture, the panels are divided by a rule, the zero line is dashed and labelled, and the three regions are marked by tick rules and named in the table, so nothing is carried by colour. Each of the four challenge plots carries a written alternative giving its sample size, its residual standard deviation by third and its average residual by third, so the reading task is answerable without seeing the picture. The pinned primary result measures 564px tall at 1366x768. Every control announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory and challenge headings as they open, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: The residual plot is the instrument: what non-constant variance does to the standard error, and what it leaves alone
simulationNotes: Observations are generated with x uniform on 10 to 90 and y = 20 + 0.5x plus normal noise whose standard deviation is 5 times a shape factor. The factor is 1 for constant variance and otherwise ramps to six times at severity 100 per cent, in one of four shapes: growing with x, shrinking with x, widest at both extremes, or widest in the middle. The last two exist because they are what makes the lesson honest: the classical standard error goes wrong to the extent that the variance lines up with leverage, which is largest at both extremes of x. Measured over 3,000 samples at n = 120 and full severity, the coverage of a nominal 95 per cent classical interval is 94.7 per cent for constant variance, 92.5 per cent for a megaphone, 86.0 per cent for variance at both extremes and 99.5 per cent - conservative rather than liberal - for variance in the middle, while the robust HC3 interval stays between 93.8 and 94.8 per cent throughout and the mean estimated slope is within 0.005 of 0.500 in every case. The tool's wording is generated from an exact model-based quantity rather than from the shape or from the simulated coverage: it computes the true standard error of the slope from the known sigma at each x and compares it with the value the classical formula is aiming at, giving ratios of 1.00, 1.05, 1.28 and 0.68 for the four patterns at full severity. The simulated coverage is reported alongside as confirmation, with its Monte Carlo error stated. No formal test for non-constant variance is computed; Breusch-Pagan and White's test are named in the page and deliberately absent, because a test invites the discussion to collapse into a threshold and because such tests are themselves sensitive to sample size. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study or dataset is involved.
